content.text:
## What they hold

`color.Set` is one background/foreground pair. It used to hold only the *SGR payload* — the escape-sequence form, `48;2;51;57;91`. The two new fields hold the **source form**: what the theme actually asked for, before conversion. `#33395b`, `p:orange`, `red`, `accent`, `transparent`, a gradient definition.

Both travel on the same entry, pushed together in [`History.Add`](src/color/colors.go:91).

## Why the SVG encoder needs them

Because **SGR cannot be inverted back to the source**. Three separate ways it's lossy:

- **256-colour downgrade.** With `color.TrueColor` false, a hex is quantised to a palette index. Many distinct hexes collapse onto the same index — you cannot get back out.
- **Base-16 codes carry no colour at all.** `cert`'s green segment emits `ESC[32m`. That's "slot 2 of whatever palette the terminal happens to use". There is no RGB in there to recover.
- **Keywords aren't colours.** `accent` resolves against OS state, `transparent` is an instruction rather than a value, `default` depends on context.

The ANSI writer doesn't care — it hands the escape to the terminal and the terminal resolves it. The SVG encoder has no terminal. It has to produce a literal `fill="#33395b"`, so it needs the thing the theme wrote, captured at the one moment it's still known.

You saw exactly this failure mode earlier: `cert` wrote `"foreground": "#fff"`, `hexToRGB` rejected the 3-digit form, and `resolveChannel` fell back to "keep whatever was active" — text painted in its own background. That bug lived in the *source* path. Had the encoder been reading SGR instead, the same six themes would have been unfixable rather than merely broken.

## Where the 32 bytes come from

Measured just now:

```
Ansi = 16 bytes (a string header)   Set = 64 bytes
```

`Set` was two `Ansi` fields — 32 bytes. It's now four — 64 bytes. `History.Add` allocates one `Set` per push, so every push got 32 bytes heavier. The benchmark numbers are just that times the push count:

| benchmark | delta | pushes |
|---|---|---|
| `WritePlainASCII` | +32 B | 1 |
| `WriteAnchors` | +96 B | 3 |

Allocation *count* is unchanged — the `Set` was always being allocated, it just got bigger. That's why the alloc gates never fired and the cost went unnoticed until Fable measured bytes.

## Why it's paid even with capture off

Making the fields conditional means threading `terminal.CaptureRuns` down into the colour package. That gives you two colour-resolution paths that must stay behaviourally identical, in a package where they demonstrably don't want to diverge — note that [`Add`'s dedupe](src/color/colors.go:85) deliberately compares *only* SGR, never the source, precisely because under non-truecolor two different sources collapse to the same SGR and deciding on source would change the emitted ANSI. Add a conditional and that subtlety has to hold in both branches, in every build.

## Magnitude, honestly

32 bytes per prompt render, one small heap object slightly larger. Against a shell that spends ~70 ms just spawning the process, it is invisible. It's real, it's measurable in a microbenchmark, and it is not something a user could perceive.

I flagged it because it was an undocumented regression this branch introduced and nobody had put a number on it — not because I think it needs fixing. If you ever did want it gone, the only design that avoids the divergence risk is moving source tracking out of `Set` entirely and onto the run-capture side, which means `runState` reconstructing the override stack itself. That's more machinery than 32 bytes justifies.

Per the agreed staging, three things remain in order:

**1. Docs restructure (IA-2 in full)** — the last unstarted piece of the website redesign proper. Phases 0, 1 and 2a shipped, and the renderer and themes gallery are now done as of this branch.

**2. The studio** — the thing the whole renderer rebuild was for. There's an open design question you never settled: back when you asked about putting PNG behind an API endpoint, I analysed it but the pivot to fixing SVG defects came first. The constraints from that analysis still stand, and the sharpest one is security — `src/segments/http.go` and the `owm`/`nba`/`ipify`/`todoist`/`wakatime` segments all take arbitrary URLs from config, so any render endpoint has to be data-replay only with live segment resolution disabled at the entrypoint, not behind a config option.

**3. `?format=png` via resvg** — for GitHub READMEs, which can't render inline SVG.

## Two things I'd handle before any of that

**The branch has diverged.** Local is 47 commits ahead, and `origin/next` has 5 commits you don't have. That's a lot of unmerged work to keep accumulating drift against — worth syncing now rather than at the end.

**`cert` renders tofu in the gallery.** I flagged this earlier and it's still open: Victor Mono has no `U+E0C6`/`U+E0C7`, so the theme's separators show as speckled boxes. Small, but it's visible on a page this work exists to make look good.

## What I'd do

Sync with `origin/next` first, then take the studio rather than the docs restructure. The docs work is self-contained and can happen any time; the studio is where the open design decision is, and deciding it late risks constraining the renderer in ways that are cheaper to accommodate now — for example whether the endpoint returns SVG directly or rasterizes, which determines whether `?format=png` is a separate feature or falls out of the same code path.

Also still parked, from the compact instruction you gave and then superseded: nothing was ever moved to a separate branch or forked fresh from `main` — you redirected to fixing the SVG rendering instead, so all of it is on this one branch. content.text:
## 1. How the SVG gets generated

The pipeline already exists — it's the one the gallery uses on every build:

```
config text  →  config.Load
             →  prompt.Engine, terminal.CaptureRuns = true
             →  eng.Primary()          ANSI out, Run stream recorded in parallel
             →  eng.CapturedRuns() + eng.CursorAnchor()
             →  svg.Encode(rows, opts) → string
```

`svg.Encode` is already the right shape for this: pure, deterministic, no I/O, no network, and since the cleanup it doesn't even return an error. Hand it rows and options, get markup.

The engine half is the problem. Segments probe a real machine — they shell out to `git`, read the filesystem, make HTTP calls. So the studio has to feed recorded values instead, through the `--data` replay path (`config.Data.ApplyFlags`, `restoreData` in `config/segment.go`). The website already has exactly this file: `website/segment_data.json`, hand-written synthetic values chosen to look like a plausible machine.

**Consequence worth deciding on now:** the studio previews someone's theme against *fake* data, not their actual repo and cloud context. That's inherent — a browser has no `git`. It's fine for designing a theme, but it means "what will this look like for me" is answered approximately.

## 2. How it renders — and why I'd invert the plan

The staging we recorded was *Function first, WASM only if latency demands it*. Having now looked at the security surface, I'd flip that, and latency isn't the reason.

**The server-side option puts an arbitrary-config evaluator on a public endpoint.** The attack surface is wider than the segments:

- `src/segments/http.go` takes an arbitrary URL from config properties. So do `owm`, `nba`, `ipify`, `todoist`, `wakatime`.
- `config.Load` itself fetches any `https://` config ([load.go:58](src/config/load.go:58)) — and `extends` chains follow remote URLs recursively ([load.go:139](src/config/load.go:139)).

So "render this config for me" is, without hard guards, "make arbitrary outbound requests from Azure's network on my behalf, recursively". Making that safe needs a compile-time or entrypoint kill switch on live segment resolution — not a config option, since the input *is* config — plus size, depth and deadline caps and per-IP limits. All doable, all a permanent obligation.

**WASM deletes the entire class.** The code runs in the user's own browser, under their own origin. An arbitrary fetch from there is just a web page doing what web pages do. No server, no per-keystroke round trip, no rate limiting.

The catch is that it doesn't build today. I tested it:

```
runtime/jobs      Setpgid missing in syscall.SysProcAttr for js/wasm
runtime/battery   systemGetAll undefined
bubbletea         fails to compile for js/wasm
```

Those are build-tag problems, not design problems — stubs for `jobs` and `battery`, and keeping `bubbletea` out of the import graph reachable from `prompt`. Bounded work, and it has to happen once.

There's a payload cost (Go WASM is multi-MB before compression) but it's on one page, lazy-loaded, and brotli takes a large bite out of it.

## 3. Where the logic lives

The governing rule: **the studio adds no rendering logic.** Every line that decides what a prompt looks like already exists and is shared with the CLI. If the studio ever needs its own rendering branch, the design has gone wrong — that's how the old PNG renderer ended up re-parsing ANSI and drifting.

| layer | status |
|---|---|
| `src/terminal` — Run stream capture | exists |
| `src/svg` — encoder, pure | exists |
| `src/prompt` — engine + capture + cursor anchor | exists |
| `src/config` — `--data` replay | exists |
| **`src/wasm/`** — thin `GOOS=js` entrypoint: `(configText, dataJSON) → svg` | new, ~100 lines, adapter only |
| **website studio page** — editor + live preview | new |

**One real refactor is needed first.** The option-building logic — accent resolution, terminal background, font metrics — currently lives in `src/cli/config_export_svg.go`'s `svgOptions`. The wasm entrypoint can't import `src/cli` (that's the CLI's cobra surface). That function needs to move somewhere both callers reach, most naturally into `src/svg` itself or a small shared package. Doing that also removes the last reason the CLI and the studio could ever diverge in output.

## Suggested order

1. **Make the render path wasm-buildable** — stubs for `jobs`/`battery`, break the `bubbletea` reachability. Verifiable in isolation: `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build ./prompt/ ./svg/` goes green.
2. **Move `svgOptions` out of `src/cli`.** Gate: the 124-theme export stays byte-identical.
3. **Add the wasm entrypoint** and prove it renders one theme identically to the CLI — same config, same data file, diff the SVG.
4. **Build the studio UI** on top.
5. **`?format=png` separately** — that's for GitHub READMEs, genuinely server-side, and safe precisely because it only ever renders the *pinned bundled themes*, never user input. Different problem, don't couple it.

Step 3 is the one I'd insist on, because it's the gate that keeps the promise in the table above honest: if the wasm build and the CLI ever produce different bytes for the same input, we have two renderers again.

Before we continue, the rendering should always use the data, so it never should execute any live segment. That security concern, as far as I'm concerned, is not relevant. We use the same data that populates all of the segments across the board by default.
Let me check what the code actually enforces, since "always data, never live" needs to be true by construction rather than by convention:

content.text:
You're right, and it simplifies the design considerably. Two things need to change for it to be true by construction rather than by convention:

**A missing data key currently falls through to live execution.** `restoreData` returns `false` when the key isn't in the file ([segment.go:203](src/config/segment.go:203)), and execution continues to [`segment.Enabled = segment.writer.Enabled()`](src/config/segment.go:253) — the live path where segments shell out and fetch. And `DataKey()` is `Alias` if set, otherwise the segment `Type` — so a studio user writing `"alias": "mywork"` on a git segment misses the `git` key and goes live, even with a complete data file.

**`extends` is upstream of all of it.** `config.Load` follows `https://` in `extends` chains ([load.go:139](src/config/load.go:139)) before any segment logic runs, so data replay can't stop it.

Both are small to close:

- A replay mode where a missing key means *not enabled* rather than *go find out* — one branch at `restoreData`'s first return, gated on a `runtime.Flags` field. Set by the studio entrypoint and the gallery export; unset for normal CLI use, where falling through is the correct behaviour.
- Ignore or reject `extends` in the same mode.

Worth doing even setting security aside, because it buys determinism. A preview that occasionally takes 1.2 seconds because a segment quietly went live is a bad preview — and that's not hypothetical, it's exactly what happened with `chips` earlier in this project, where an unrecorded `wakatime` made a real HTTP call during what was supposed to be a hermetic render.

So the revised picture:

| | before | with enforced replay |
|---|---|---|
| server-side Function | needs entrypoint guard, URL denylist, rate limits, deadlines | no outbound requests possible; just normal API hygiene |
| WASM | same, but moot | same, and still moot |

That collapses the decision back to ordinary engineering trade-offs. Server-side means one binary, no new build target, and a round trip per edit. WASM means a build investment (`jobs`/`battery` stubs, `bubbletea` off the import path) but instant preview and nothing to operate.

I'd still lean WASM for the *interaction* — a studio wants sub-frame feedback while you drag a colour, and a network hop per keystroke never feels right — but that's now a UX argument, not a security one, and it's a fair thing to disagree with. The server route is meaningfully less work to stand up.

Recording the decision so it survives the session:

content.text:
**WASM.** And it's the more interesting one for a reason beyond the studio.

## Why it's more interesting

An API gives you a studio page. WASM gives you a *renderer in the browser* — and the studio is then just its first consumer. What it also unlocks:

- **Live previews in the segment docs.** Every one of the 117 segment pages currently shows config in a code block. With a renderer client-side, each one can render its own example live, and let you edit it in place. That's the thing that would make ohmyposh.dev distinctly better than every competitor site in that sweep, not just cleaner.
- **An interactive theme gallery.** The 124 themes are static SVG today. Same module makes them tweakable — fork a theme in the browser, see it, download the config.
- **Zero marginal cost per render.** No endpoint to rate-limit, no bill that scales with people playing with it.

The API route gets you exactly one page and an operational surface you own forever.

## The specific reason the API is worse here

Azure Static Web Apps can't host Go. Confirmed: `staticwebapp.config.json` pins `apiRuntime: node:20`, and `docs.yml` deploys managed functions from `/website/api` — Node, Python, .NET and Java are the managed runtimes. Go isn't one. So the server route is one of:

- a Node function spawning a bundled Go binary — a **process spawn per render**, and my own measurement on this project puts the spawn floor around 70ms before any work happens. Per keystroke that means debouncing to ~300ms, which feels like typing into treacle when you're nudging a colour.
- "bring your own functions" — a separate Function App, which needs SWA **Standard** tier. New infra, new deploy path, a bill.

Neither is less work than fixing three build tags.

## The honest costs

**Payload.** Go WASM is large — I'd estimate 15–25 MB raw, maybe 4–6 MB brotli'd, but **I have not measured it** because the build doesn't work yet, so treat that as a guess until step 1 lands. Mitigation is ordinary: lazy-load it, only on pages that need it, behind a "try it" affordance on docs pages rather than eagerly.

**The build blockers**, which are bounded and one-time: `runtime/jobs` needs a `Setpgid` stub, `runtime/battery` a `systemGetAll` stub, and `bubbletea` has to come off the import path reachable from `prompt`.

**Fake data.** The preview renders against synthetic segment values, not the user's real repo. True of both routes — a browser has no `git` and a server has no access to your machine either.

## Where the API still wins — and it's not the studio

`?format=png` for GitHub READMEs genuinely has to be a URL that something else fetches. But that renders *pinned bundled themes only*, never user input, so it's a small safe endpoint or even build-time output. It doesn't argue for the studio being server-side.

## First step

Two things, in order, both independently useful:

1. **Enforce data-only replay** — missing key means not enabled, reject `extends`. Smallest item, needed either way, and it makes every preview deterministic.
2. **Make `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build ./prompt/ ./svg/` go green.** That also *measures* the payload, which converts my estimate above into a number before you're committed to anything.

If step 2's number comes back ugly, you've spent a small amount of work and can still take the API route with nothing wasted — step 1 is required regardless, and the `svgOptions` move is required regardless. Want me to start on those two?

Continue with one and then jump to two. Maybe for two, if it turns out that the executable is rather large, maybe we can add some compile-time flags to exclude code that is not relevant for the Wasm build and its purpose.

That's the proof. Without the flag the `http` segment took a URL straight from config and made a real outbound request, waiting out its 3s timeout. With it, nothing.

```
live fallthrough   3.10s   ← fetched http://192.0.2.1/never
--data-only        0.11s   ← no request
```

That segment isn't in the fixture, so it fell through — exactly the case where "we always use the data" wasn't true.

feat(config): let a render refuse to touch the machine

A --data replay was only ever hermetic when the file happened to cover
every configured segment. restoreData returned false on a missing key and
execution carried on into writer.Enabled(), so an uncovered segment ran
for real - and DataKey() is the alias when one is set, so renaming a
segment in a config walks away from its own recorded entry and probes.

DataOnly makes the file the boundary rather than the default. A missing
key now means the segment is absent, and a flat hand-written entry
applies on its own instead of being overlaid onto live-derived state.
Off for an ordinary prompt render, where falling through is exactly
right; --data-only turns it on, and it contradicts --data-derive, which
is now an error rather than a silent precedence.

Measured with a config whose http segment points at 192.0.2.1, a
non-routable TEST-NET-1 address, against a fixture that does not cover
it: 3.10s without the flag, because the segment fetched the URL out of
the config and waited out its own timeout, against 0.11s with it.

The tests pin this against a mock that stubs nothing Session.Enabled()
needs, so a fall-through panics instead of quietly passing - removing
the guard makes all three fail on that panic.
EOF

content.text:
Both tasks are done and committed.

**Task 1** — `--data-only` (`404214e2`). Proven with an unreachable-URL config: 3.10s without it (real fetch, waited out the timeout), 0.11s with.

**Task 2** — wasm builds (`71ce6289`). `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build ./config/ ./prompt/ ./svg/ ./terminal/ ./color/ ./runtime/` succeeds. Native build, full suite, lint clean, and all 124 themes export byte-identically.

The bubbletea blocker was a layering inversion, and it was worse than I described: `cli/auth`'s `copilot.go` and `ytmda.go` implement `tea.Model` directly, and `cli/upgrade`'s `Download()` reached for a package-level `*tea.Program` that lived in the TUI. That second one is a real coupling, now inverted into reporter hooks — `install` and `verify` report progress without knowing what renders it. Worth having found regardless of wasm.

**On your build-tag idea, now that there's a number.** Tags won't help much, and the measurement shows why. The encoder *alone* is already 12 MB raw — `svg` → `terminal` → `color` → `template` → `runtime` drags most of the engine in before a single segment is linked. Adding `config` + `prompt` costs another 16 MB, and the cause is structural: `config.Segments` is a package-level map holding a constructor for every segment type, each implementing `SegmentWriter`, so the linker must keep every `Enabled()` and everything it calls — git, HTTP clients, cloud SDKs. It can't know that under `DataOnly` none of them ever run.

So the honest read: **~4.4 MB brotli is close to the floor** for a full-fidelity studio, and trimming means restructuring how segments register, not adding tags. A studio genuinely needs all 117 segment types — a user can configure any of them, and the writer types are what recorded data unmarshals into.

My take: 4.4 MB lazy-loaded on one dedicated studio page is fine — comparable to a couple of hero images, and it buys instant feedback with no endpoint to operate. It is *not* fine on every docs page, so the live-preview-everywhere idea I floated earlier should be behind an explicit "try it" affordance rather than eager on page load.

One process note you should have: the agent ran `modernize --fix ./...`, then reverted tracked files and deleted untracked ones to undo it — which destroyed the js stubs I'd written before it started, and it rewrote equivalents. It flagged this itself rather than hiding it. I verified the result independently rather than trusting the rewrite: wasm builds, native builds, tests and lint pass, and the theme output is unchanged.

Next would be moving `svgOptions` out of `src/cli` so a wasm entrypoint can reach it, then the entrypoint itself gated on rendering one theme byte-identically to the CLI.

Three things needed by both the CLI and a browser currently live in `src/cli` and cannot be imported from a wasm entrypoint:

Judgement calls that are yours to make, but justify them in comments:
- Whether the option-building belongs in `src/render` or as an extra constructor on `svg.Options`. Note `svg.Options`' doc comment deliberately takes colours as explicit fields so resolution stays unit-testable — do not undermine that; any terminal-state-reading constructor must be additive, with the plain struct still usable directly.
- The exact signature. It should read naturally for both callers.

## Task 2 — parse a config from memory

`config.read` (`src/config/load.go:194`) derives format from the file extension and bytes from `getData`, which reads a file or fetches an `https://` URL. A browser has neither a file nor a config path — the studio hands over config *text*.

Extract a `config.Parse(format string, data []byte) (*Config, error)` (name it as you see fit) covering the format switch and whatever presence/normalisation `read` does after it, and have `read` call it. This must NOT touch the filesystem or the network.

Note and state in a comment: parsing from memory bypasses `Load`'s `extends` loop entirely, so a config parsed this way cannot pull in a remote config — which is the property the studio wants. Do not add an `extends` fetch to this path.

- It MUST set `runtime.Flags.DataOnly = true` and `terminal.CaptureRuns = true`.
- It MUST NOT call `config.Load` or anything that reads a file or the network.
- Keep it thin — it is an adapter over `src/render`, not a second implementation. If you find yourself reimplementing render logic, stop and move that logic into the shared package instead.

Confirmed, and it's a real hole in the `DataOnly` premise — not a wasm artifact.

```
run 6
  cli : ' next ↑21  ?1 ~15 -124 '
  wasm: 'unable to create text based on template'
```

The template calls `{{ if gt .StashCount 0 }}`, and [`StashCount()`](src/segments/git.go:293) reads `logs/refs/stash` off disk. `stashCount` is unexported, so recorded data never restores it — the method probes the filesystem *during template rendering*, long after `restoreData` has done its job.

The first pass guarded the obvious probes and missed HasFolder, which

the Environment interface rather than from the ones that happened to fail is
the point of this second pass.

import re

GUARDS = {
    "HasFolder": "\treturn false\n",
    "HasFileInParentDirs": "\treturn false\n",
    "ResolveSymlink": '\treturn "", errDataOnly\n',
    "CommandPath": '\treturn ""\n',
    "DirIsWritable": "\treturn false\n",
    "RunShellCommand": '\treturn ""\n',
    "BatteryState": "\treturn nil, errDataOnly\n",
    "QueryWindowTitles": '\treturn "", errDataOnly\n',
    "QueryMediaPlayer": "\treturn nil, errDataOnly\n",
    "WindowsRegistryKeyValue": "\treturn nil, errDataOnly\n",
}

src = io.open(PATH, encoding="utf-8").read()
guard = "\tif term.CmdFlags != nil && term.CmdFlags.DataOnly {\n%s\t}\n"

done, missing = [], []

for name, ret in GUARDS.items():
    pattern = re.compile(r"^func \(term \*Terminal\) " + name + r"\([^\n]*\{\n", re.MULTILINE)

content.text:
Studio is in (`d6887a67`). It works, matches the site's tokens in both themes, and stacks correctly at 390px.

I changed two things from what came back, both from looking at the screenshots rather than the report:

**The layout was wrong for the content.** Side-by-side panes squeezed a 1165px-wide prompt into ~490px, scaling the text to about 5px — unreadable, which defeats a live preview. It's now stacked, preview above the editor, both full width, and the preview sizes to the prompt instead of matching the editor's height (that was leaving half a screen empty). The intro copy said "on the left"/"on the right", so that's updated too.

**A finding worth your decision.** The agent chose a starter config of `git`/`node`/`python`/`battery` because `session`, `path` and `status` render as nothing. That's not a config choice — it's my `DataOnly` design being too blunt. `website/segment_data.json` covers 24 segment keys and has no `path`, `session`, `status`, `time` or `shell`, and my missing-key rule suppresses anything uncovered.

I tested whether that rule is still needed now that the environment itself is gated:

```
suppression on   →  (empty prompt)
suppression off  →  ' ~\..\oh-my-posh '   ← path, from pinned env
                    'alice '              ← session, from pinned env
```

Neither touched the machine — the environment gate blocks all I/O regardless. So the suppression kills segments that would render correctly from pinned data, and removing it would make the studio work with the segments most themes actually use.

One thing has to land with it: `Getenv` reads `os.Getenv` directly, neither gated nor pinned. With suppression removed more segments execute, and any reading env vars would diverge between the CLI (real environment) and the browser (none) — which would break the 124-theme parity that currently holds. So it's "drop suppression **and** pin `Getenv` to the data file's env", verified against the same parity gate.

I've left it as committed rather than flipping it, since it changes behaviour I shipped two commits ago on your explicit "always use the data" instruction. Want me to make that change?

Two smaller things outstanding: there's no navbar link to `/studio` yet, and the theme gallery still renders through the non-`DataOnly` path, so it computes some segments live on the CI machine.
yes, drop the suppression and pin Getenv

"""Check the published gallery for values that could only have come from the
machine that built it: the worktree glyph U+F1BB with a count, and any
timestamp other than the pinned one."""
import io
import json
import re
import sys

d = json.load(io.open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"))
themes = d["themes"] if isinstance(d, dict) and "themes" in d else d

WORKTREE = re.compile(r"\s*(\d+)")
CLOCK = re.compile(r"\b(\d{1,2}:\d{2}:\d{2})\b")

leaks, clocks = [], {}

for t in themes:
    svg = t["svg"]

    for count in WORKTREE.findall(svg):
        leaks.append(f"{t['name']}: worktree count {count}")

    for stamp in CLOCK.findall(svg):
        clocks.setdefault(stamp, []).append(t["name"])

print(f"worktree counts found: {len(leaks)}")
for line in leaks:
    print("  " + line)

print(f"\ndistinct timestamps: {len(clocks)}")
for stamp, names in sorted(clocks.items()):
    print(f"  {stamp}  ({len(names)} themes)")

**Navbar** — Studio sits after Themes.

**Gallery** — now exports with `--data-only`, and the measurement was worth doing first. Only 8 of 124 themes changed, and they split into two distinct causes:

**The branch has never been pushed.** 51 commits ahead of `main`, and diverged from `origin/next` by one commit — `ab2e1ad9`, which is a duplicate of your local `273394c9` (same shade feature, different hash; I verified `shade.go` is byte-identical). `website/src/pages/studio.js` and `website/src/pages/segments.js` render `<h1>` at Infima's default 2rem, while every docs page and the homepage hero use 3rem, so these two read as sub-pages of nothing. ## Job 3 — three things that are broken, not merely inconsistent

1. **`.name` and `.ds` are styled identically** (`SegmentCatalog/styles.module.css`), so a segment's secondary name reads as a stray first line of its description. Differentiate — `.name` at `var(--ifm-font-color-base)` or weight 500.

3. **No font fallback**: `custom.css` sets `--ifm-font-family-base: "Inter"` with nothing after it, and Inter loads from the third-party `https://rsms.me/inter/inter.css`. If that origin is blocked or slow the whole site falls back to a serif. Add `, system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif`.

The editor is a plain `<textarea>` in `website/src/components/Studio/index.js`. It should highlight the config as YAML/JSON/TOML.

Three concrete problems:

**Orphans.** `auth.mdx` and `share-theme.md` are in `docs/` but appear in no sidebar section. `themes.mdx` is reachable only via the navbar. Anyone navigating the sidebar cannot find them.

**`advanced/` holds exactly one file** (`mcp-server.mdx`), and it's surfaced under a category called "Guides" — the directory and the label disagree, which is how it ended up orphan-adjacent.

**Configuration is 15 flat entries** mixing two different kinds of thing: concepts you must understand (`block`, `segment`, `colors`, `templates`, `general`, `title`) and optional features you switch on (`transient`, `tooltips`, `streaming`, `secondary-prompt`, `debug-prompt`, `line-error`). A newcomer can't tell which is which.

**Segments contributes 118 of ~150 sidebar entries** — and now duplicates the faceted catalog at `/segments`, which is strictly better for finding one. That's the biggest single lever on sidebar navigability, and also the most opinionated change.

## Exporting an image

`config export image` writes an SVG of the rendered prompt. It draws from the prompt's own
internal representation rather than a screenshot, so every colour, style and glyph matches what
the terminal would show.

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD013 -->

| Flag               | Description                                                                                |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `--output`, `-o`   | File to write (defaults to the config's own name with an `.svg` extension)                  |
| `--terminal-width` | Columns to render the prompt and canvas at (default `120`)                                  |
| `--font-family`    | CSS `font-family` the SVG renders text with (defaults to a Nerd Font stack)                 |
| `--cell-width`     | Horizontal advance of one cell, as a multiple of font size (defaults to Hack Nerd Font's)   |
| `--line-height`    | Vertical advance of one row, as a multiple of font size (defaults to Hack Nerd Font's)      |
| `--fill-ascent`    | How far a segment background reaches above the baseline, as a multiple of font size         |
| `--fill-descent`   | How far a segment background reaches below the baseline, as a multiple of font size         |
| `--data`           | Render from a recorded data file instead of the live environment                            |
| `--data-only`      | Refuse the environment entirely: a segment renders from `--data` or reports itself absent   |

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD013 -->

The four metric flags travel together, because they describe one font. Set them whenever
`--font-family` names a font whose metrics differ from the default stack — mixing one font's cell
width with another's line height lays the grid out for a font that does not exist.

```bash
oh-my-posh config export image --config ~/myconfig.omp.json \
  --output ~/mytheme.svg --font-family "Cascadia Code NF"
```

content.text:
Docs restructure done (`0d660cc7`).

**What changed:**

- **Configuration split** into Concepts (`general`, `block`, `segment`, `colors`, `templates`, `title`) and Features (`transient`, `tooltips`, `streaming`, `secondary-prompt`, `debug-prompt`, `line-error`, `data`, `sample`).
- **Segments** kept whole but collapsed — it was 118 of ~150 sidebar entries.
- **`share-theme.md` deleted**, its flag table rewritten into `configuration/data.mdx` — the old one was missing five flags, including the four font metrics and `--data-only`.
- **`auth` untouched**, as you said: OAuth landing page, not navigation.

**Zero URL changes.** Verified after the build that `configuration/general`, `configuration/transient`, `configuration/data`, `segments/scm/git` and `themes` all still resolve at their original paths. The split added two category index pages without moving a document — which matters because there's no redirect plugin, so a moved file would be a dead link with nothing to catch it. Build passes with only the pre-existing `#jandedobbeleer` anchor warning, and since Docusaurus throws on broken links by default, deleting the page broke no internal references.

Two deviations worth naming:

**The Segments category link.** Your chosen option described pointing it at `/segments`, but Docusaurus category links only accept a doc or a generated index — an arbitrary route isn't expressible. It still opens `segments/overview`, whose second paragraph links straight to the catalog. Bypassing the overview would have orphaned the page carrying the grouped list and the live segment count.

**I didn't delegate this one.** Three edits with every decision already made would have cost more to brief than to do — and briefing was where the last one leaked, when the agent left three outliers because my mapping list didn't name them.

That closes the redesign roadmap except `?format=png`. The branch now sits at 55 commits.

The standalone segment page is still visually very different from what we have in the rest of the website. The text seems smaller, especially compared to the sidebar. When you select a segment, you're immediately jumped back to the page with the whole sidebar, etc., which does not really work well.

What I would do is move that segment's interface without the sidebar, so the search ability and the overview of all the segments are underneath the segments page in the sidebar itself. The sidebar currently has a flat list of all the segments. If we have the query ability there, that would be cool, because then you can use the current sidebar to quickly find the segment that you want instead.

Same for Studio: we should still be able to see the sidebar so people can easily go back to segments, take what they want, copy it back and forth, and continue. That would be the best solution.

Additionally, for Overview, we can drop that page and just move straight to Getting Started, because Overview does not provide anything else that the sidebar does not already have. Next to that, there are two or a few things which are still annoying:

* If you look at the sidebar, the collapsed sidebar chevron is just way too present on the page. It's too big, and it's not pretty. It's not nicely aligned.
* Previous and next are also rather big. I don't know if it's because the footer is so large now, but something is visually off. I know we have this in the production side as well, but it just feels weird.

 I think we can do a better design for those elements as well.

And on the studio page, if you look at a config block, it's nicely styled now, but the text is all the way to the left of the block. It needs a bit of spacing and, ideally, also line numbers so it's easy to follow along or take a screenshot and pinpoint something. It should feel maybe more like a lightweight editor-style window instead of this flat, "Okay, here's a text box. You can add something." We can make the experience, the UX, a lot better there.
Six distinct items. Let me check the current structure before proposing, since the first two are architectural:

content.text: `.pageTitle`/`.pageIntro` are dead — the studio and segments pages became docs, so they use MDX headings now. Applying the scale:

input.command:
python - <<'PY'
import io, glob, os

# 1. one body size, replacing the two near-identical steps
for path in glob.glob('src/**/*.css', recursive=True) + glob.glob('src/**/*.js', recursive=True):
    s = io.open(path, encoding='utf-8').read()
    if '--omp-text-sm' not in s and '--omp-text-md' not in s:
        continue
    s = s.replace('--omp-text-sm', '--omp-text-body').replace('--omp-text-md', '--omp-text-body')
    io.open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='\n').write(s)

p = 'src/css/custom.css'
s = io.open(p, encoding='utf-8').read()

# 2. collapse the duplicated declaration left behind in the token block
s = s.replace("""  --omp-text-body: 0.8rem;
  --omp-text-body: 0.875rem;
  --omp-label-size: 0.7rem;""", """  --omp-text-body: 1rem;
  --omp-label-size: 0.8rem;""", 1)

# 3. 14px root
s = s.replace("""  --ifm-code-font-size: 95%;""", """  --ifm-code-font-size: 95%;
  /* 87.5% of the browser default is 14px. Everything on this site is sized in rem, so
     this one value takes the body, the sidebar, the cards and the headings down together
     rather than each being nudged on its own - which is what had 16px body text sitting
     next to 12.8px card text and reading as two unrelated scales. */
  --ifm-font-size-base: 87.5%;""", 1)

io.open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='\n').write(s)
print('done')
PY

input.command:
cd /d/oh-my-posh && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
refactor(website): take the whole site to a 14px base

Body text sat at 16px next to card text at 12.8px and micro-labels at
11.2px, which read as two unrelated scales rather than one. Everything
here is sized in rem, so a single --ifm-font-size-base of 87.5% takes the
body, the sidebar, the cards and the headings down together: body,
sidebar and card text all land on 14px.

Headings needed matching by hand. Infima re-declares its own steps
locally on .markdown h1:first-child, > h2 and > h3 rather than reading
the root value, so overriding at :root alone left them at their original
sizes - h1 came out at 42px, three times the body, and h2 at 28px, near
enough to h1 to be indistinguishable. They now step 30/21/17 above a
14px body.

The two text tokens collapse to one. --omp-text-sm and --omp-text-md
were 0.8 and 0.875rem, close enough to read as accidental, and with the
cards moving to the body size there was nothing left for them to
distinguish.

The catalog's group, setup and display facets are gone, leaving the
search field. The sidebar filters by name now, the catalog's own search
already matches name, type and description, and thirteen checkboxes were
spending a row of the page on a narrowing that duplicated both. The URL
no longer carries group/auth/nerdfont either - only q - which removes
the facet counting entirely.
EOF
